title: Static-Field Shielding of Bosonic Molecules: Evaporation to Degeneracy and Self-Bound Droplets
authors: Jongheum Jung, Laura Futamura, Matteo Ciardi, Jason Rosenberg, Youssef Aziz Alaoui, Yukai Lu, Thomas Pohl, Waseem S. Bakr
abstract: The strong, tunable dipolar interactions of ultracold molecules make them a powerful platform for quantum many-body physics, but reaching degeneracy by evaporative cooling requires suppressing inelastic collisions. Microwave collisional shielding has enabled the preparation of degenerate Fermi gases and Bose-Einstein condensates of polar molecules, whereas static electric field shielding has been limited to fermionic species, which are less prone to inelastic loss. We demonstrate static-field Förster shielding of bosonic $^{23}$Na$^{87}$Rb molecules, suppressing two-body loss by up to four orders of magnitude. Within a bound-state-free electric-field window, three-body loss is also strongly suppressed, enabling efficient evaporation. Evaporating with an efficiency of 2.09(9), we increase the phase-space density of the gas by two orders of magnitude, reaching degeneracy with 7200(1000) molecules. We observe self-bound droplets at the end of evaporation over a wide range of field strengths, emerging from either degenerate or non-degenerate parent gases. We perform Path Integral Monte Carlo simulations, which suggest that the observed droplets are filamentary in nature, and find good agreement with the experimentally observed droplet formation temperatures. Our results establish Förster shielding as a single-field route to prepare degenerate gases and self-bound droplets of bosonic polar molecules.
summary: This paper reports on using static electric fields to achieve Förster shielding in bosonic dipolar molecules, effectively suppressing molecular loss channels. By operating in a specific field window, the researchers enabled efficient evaporative cooling to quantum degeneracy and successfully observed the formation of self-bound quantum droplets. This establishes a robust, single-field technique for preparing and studying highly correlated quantum matter.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving quantum degeneracy and observing self-bound droplets in bosonic molecules while suppressing inelastic collisions, particularly three-body loss.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that static-field Förster shielding can suppress two-body loss by four orders of magnitude and, crucially, suppress three-body loss in a bound-state-free window, enabling efficient evaporative cooling to degeneracy.
method: The study combines experimental measurements of loss rates (two-body and three-body) during evaporative cooling with theoretical modeling, including Path Integral Monte Carlo simulations.
model_or_system: The system involves ultracold bosonic $^{23}	ext{Na}^{87}	ext{Rb}$ molecules with tunable dipolar interactions, trapped in an optical dipole trap and controlled by a static electric field to induce Förster shielding.
key_observables: Two-body and three-body loss rate coefficients ($ eta_{	ext{loss}}$, $L_3$), phase-space density, molecule number, and observation of self-bound droplets.
important_parameters: The Föster defect ($\Delta F$) controls the shielding; the study focuses on the 'bound-state-free electric-field window' for optimal cooling.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the applicability of kinetic models for loss rates and uses simplified Gaussian forms for droplet decay dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup and energy level diagrams near the Föster resonance; subsequent figures show the dependence of two-body loss rates on the field defect and the evolution of the gas during evaporation.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the necessity of shielding to suppress two-body loss, then demonstrating that operating in a bound-state-free window also suppresses three-body loss, which allows for efficient evaporative cooling to degeneracy, culminating in the observation and characterization of self-bound droplets.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controllable, single-field mechanism (Förster shielding) to manage the complex loss channels (two-body and three-body) inherent in highly interacting dipolar quantum gases, which is a major frontier in AMO physics.
